title: Melody Inn combo and rock and roll
summary: He recalls his combo at the Melody Inn, a rock and roll drummer sitting in, his dislike of rock and roll, and the old cymbal pedal.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Now when I was working down here at the Melody Inn. We had a little combo down there. Saxophone player that played with me down there. Sunday. Harold Dajon. Harold Dajon was on sax. Same piano player was there with me playing. Simon Fraser.
Not Simon Fraser. That was a cousin or something like that. Smitty. Smitty. I can't think he was last name. The one that was that Sunday. And had a fella by the name of Lionel Favos playing trumpet.
That guitar player huh wasn't it? Huh? Wasn't that guitar player too? No.
George Daniel started over there with me.

I was about to say. But then some kind of humbug George Daniel and the man had a George Quick. So I had to get him a piano player. So I got him a piano player. And we used to play all kind of type of music. So one night, I hope I know you might have seen Ed Butterson around there. He's a rock and roll. Mr. Boo. Oh I heard of him. He was a Betty Boo. Freddie Boo or Betty Boo. I don't know anyway. He came down there. Him and his drummer. Well, he asked. The piano player could he play a number. Told him yeah. Drum player said, Oh, let's see then. Well, for the kind of type of music they played amongst them two. You understand the idea. Just them two that rock and roll stuff. After they got you to play piano. This fellow booed. People would clap for him. Well, just then. One of those women came and asked for a number. I forget just about what number it was anyway. It was a Dixieland number and then we played all kind of type of music down there. We played a little rock and roll down there. So piano player told him to sit in. Go ahead. Play that. You can sit in with the band. A while I go take a smoke. Drum player he wanted to get us. No, sit down there. I said. If you want to answer, go ahead. You were talking about some job down for the rock and roll. Was that place called High Del? High Del. Down around the clay bank. I remember. High Del's play. So we let them play. And Spinner and I went to take a smoke on the outside. And when we came back he said, ah, come on man. Say yeah. See. We can't play that type of music. And I looked at him and I said, well you support being a musician. You support being a musician. I said, you ought to be able to play any kind of type of music if you're a musician. But see that a lot of rock and roll stuff, that's nothing but the, I don't know what to call it. I think it stinks. If you want to know the truth about it. I can't see no rock and roll music because to me the horns are not tuned. They don't sound like they're in tune to me. And to play rock and roll music, you got to have a good singer. And you got to have a fire play guitar and clown. Now if you got that you got that. But that's what the people crazy about. I mean the younger generation come today. But for it when they come down to musician you can't call a new musician. Now without, without knocking a man or without trying to flick my head fat down with no. Man made a fortune. Yeah. But what does he got? What does he got? Outside one boy in that band, because that's the get-off man. Outside that disco band. Yeah. And George Dino was always talking about him, that he doesn't know one chord from another, but he's making a million dollars. He don't know a chord, he don't know a chord, he don't know a chord, but two keys. Outside of that he's lost. He's got something that people want so I guess this. But he got what the public want. Yeah, so yeah. He made a fortune. Yeah. Well anytime you tell him to sit in a band, he can't sit in a band. No he doesn't. And what is rock and roll? Rock and roll with one beat. It's a one beat number. Yeah. Well I was going to ask about that old cymbal when you had the little cymbal fastened to the foot pedal. And it always hit, every time you hit the bass drum. Every time you hit the bass drum, it had a little, something like a piece of metal. Yeah I remember those things. It would hit that ching, ching, ching. So it was always on the beat, not the after beat with that. No, no, always on the beat. Now I wondered in the parade bands, the bass drummer now hits on the beat of the bass drum and the cymbal after the cymbal. So boom, boom, boom, right. That's right. In the old days, did they ever hit like they did on that bass drum and the pedal at the same time with the cymbal together? Yeah, yeah, yeah. Did they ever hit the cymbal? See that point? Yeah. The cymbal and the bass drum together somehow. Yeah. That's what I wondered. Now they usually hit it after. Yeah, one after beat, yeah. Mostly in the old band, they started like that. Both the bass drum and the cymbal, the hands right together. Yeah, yeah. But then your snare drum, when you had that cymbal there, you'd come in on after beats. That's right. On your big cymbal on your snare drum. That's right.
